title: Missourians Reject Measure That Threatened to Kill Citizen-Led Ballot Initiatives
author: Pascal Sabino
content:
Missouri voters on Tuesday overwhelmingly rejected an effort by Republican
lawmakers to drastically raise the threshold for passing citizen ballot
measures—which in recent years have allowed Missourians to legalize marijuana,
raise the minimum wage, guarantee paid sick leave, expand Medicaid, and revoke
the state’s strict abortion ban, all over the objections of state GOP
officials.

Angered by these reforms, Republicans who dominate Missouri’s legislature put
Amendment 4 on Tuesday’s ballot to try and mandate that future citizen-led
initiatives win majorities in each of the state’s eight congressional
districts, as opposed to the statewide majority vote that is currently
required. Notably, the same rules would not have applied to measures that the
legislature sends to the ballot, and critics say that carveout helped rally
voters against the restriction.

Under those proposed rules, all five popular initiatives that Missouri voters
have approved since 2020 would have failed, [an analysis by _Bolts_
found](https://boltsmag.org/missouri-amendment-on-ballot-initiatives/) last
year.

Missouri activists who worked to pass these reforms in recent years had warned
that the new rules would spell the end of the citizen-led initiatives in the
state.

"It would have neutered the process altogether. Nothing would ever pass again.
Missouri voters are just smarter than that,” said Mallory Rusch, executive
director of Empower Missouri, an organization that backed measures to expand
medicaid and raise the minimum wage. “I'm really glad that Missouri voters saw
that this was really designed to trick them into giving up their own power.”

The defeat of Amendment 4 was among the most decisive votes in recent history,
with [80 percent of voters](https://enr.sos.mo.gov/) opposing the restriction.

Republican lawmakers sent Amendment 4 to the ballot during a special
legislative session called last September by Governor Mike Kehoe that largely
focused on further bolstering GOP control of the state. During that special
session, Republicans also pushed through a mid-decade redistricting plan that
eliminated the Kansas City-based congressional district held by Emanuel
Cleaver, a Black Democrat, by splitting it into three other districts
dominated by Republicans.

Ahead of Tuesday’s election, Missouri’s Republican secretary of state, Denny
Hoskins, [blocked](https://missouriindependent.com/2026/08/04/missouri-
redistricting-referendum-blocked-by-secretary-of-state-drawing-lawsuit/) a
public referendum on the new maps, declaring that  citizen-led petitions to
challenge redistricting were unconstitutional. Hoskins refused to even say
whether citizens had gathered enough valid signatures to qualify for the
November ballot, telling reporters, “Whether they had one signature or 500
million signatures doesn’t really matter.”

Last year’s gerrymandering was itself a sign of how hard Missouri Republicans
have worked to sidestep citizen ballot initiatives. In 2018, voters
overwhelmingly approved a measure to establish a bipartisan redistricting
commission and ban lobbyists from making gifts to legislators over $5. But
then two years later, legislators placed an item on the ballot to repeal the
redistricting reforms—a ballot measure that [narrowly passed that
year](https://missouriindependent.com/2020/11/04/voters-repeal-clean-missouri-
redistricting-plan-they-enacted-in-2018/), and which reform advocates argue
contained language designed to confuse voters.

Republicans have held a majority in both legislative chambers in Missouri
since 2003, and have had a supermajority in the legislature for over a decade.
Citizen-led referendums have long been the only avenue for challenging the
state’s Republican leaders, who have also sought to undo many of the recent
reforms won by popular initiatives. For instance, GOP lawmakers last summer
[repealed the 2024 ballot measure that guaranteed paid sick
leave](https://missouriindependent.com/2025/08/29/missouri-voters-expanded-
paid-sick-leave-the-gop-undid-it-and-the-repeal-just-took-effect/), since the
reform was not an amendment to the state constitution—which would require a
majority vote from Missourians to repeal.

Bids to weaken direct democracy have become a feature of the Republican
playbook for limiting opposition in states they control, with conservative
lawmakers pushing to restrict citizen-initiated referendums in
[Arkansas](https://boltsmag.org/direct-democracy-roundtable-ohio-arkansas-
idaho/), [Florida](https://boltsmag.org/florida-new-restrictions-on-ballot-
initiative-process/) and [Oklahoma](https://boltsmag.org/oklahoma-restricts-
ballot-initiative-process/) in recent years. Some of these new restrictions,
like in Florida, have made it harder to qualify an item on the ballot by
increasing the burden for collecting signatures while also creating harsh
criminal penalties for common clerical errors and routine outreach activities.
In other states, like
[North](https://ballotpedia.org/North_Dakota_Constitutional_Measure_1,_60%25_Vote_Requirement_for_Constitutional_Amendments_Measure_\(2026\))
and [South
Dakota](https://ballotpedia.org/South_Dakota_Constitutional_Amendment_L,_60%25_Vote_Requirement_for_Constitutional_Amendments_Measure_\(2026\)),
Republican legislators have pushed to require a supermajority in order to
approve some initiatives.

Advocates who came together to defeat Amendment 4 in Missouri are now hoping
to safeguard the state’s popular initiative system from future meddling by
legislators. Organizers with the Respect Missouri Voters campaign are now
using the very tool in question—the citizen-led initiative—to push for new
rules banning state lawmakers from restricting the ballot measure process and
limiting them from weakening future measures that voters approve. They
submitted over 367,000 signatures in support of the initiative by the deadline
in May, more than double the amount needed to qualify the proposed measure for
the ballot.

But on Tuesday, Hoskins announced that he was also [rejecting that
initiative](https://missouriindependent.com/2026/08/04/missouri-redistricting-
referendum-blocked-by-secretary-of-state-drawing-lawsuit/) and would not
certify signatures gathered by the campaign, setting up a legal battle to
decide whether this amendment and redistricting reforms will appear on the
November ballot.  

“Voters are hungry to have a clear, fair, and transparent process to decide
the future of our state,” said Benjamin Singer, the director of the Respect
Missouri Voters campaign. “It's no surprise that when we have more momentum
than ever, as shown by voters defeating Amendment 4, that politicians continue
to double down and attack to try to prevent voters from having a say. But we
are confident that voters will prevail over these attacks.”
